While induction therapy may reduce the incidence and severity of acute rejection, and allow for a delay in calcineurin in- hibitor therapy, there is an increased risk of infection and of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease.2,3,5,10 Anti- lymphocyte immunoglobulins and muromonab-CD3 have been used; the interleukin-2 receptor antibodies basilixi- mab and daclizumab are increasingly used,1,2,10 although experience with these drugs in lung transplantation is lim- ited.11 Alemtuzumab is under investigation for induc- tion;1,2,10,11 preliminary results are promising. Corticoster- oids remain a mainstay in lung transplantation,5,10-12 although corticosteroid-free regimens have been investi- gated, with promising results, and further study is warrant- ed.11,12 Sirolimus has been investigated in lung transplan- tation, but its early use as a primary immunosuppressant is not recommended due to its potent antifibrotic effects;1,2 sirolimus may also induce pulmonary toxicity.10 Cases of fatal anastomotic dehiscence have been reported, and con- cerns about wound healing complications have led to rec- ommendations to only use sirolimus after initial airway bronchial wound healing is completed, or not until at least 3 months after transplant.10 Everolimus is also under in- vestigation for adjunctive use in lung transplantation.10,11 Acute rejection occurs more frequently with lung trans- plants than with other solid organ transplants;1,13 from ear- ly reports in 60 to 100% of cases, incidence has apparently decreased to about 35% in those receiving induction ther- apy and about 45% in those without induction therapy,10 although some centres have reported figures as high as 85%.13 High doses of intravenous corticosteroids are gen- erally used to control acute episodes of rejection.3,7,10,13 Corticosteroid-refractory rejection demands further inter- vention, although no consensus exists. Evidence supports the conversion of ciclosporin to tacrolimus for patients with persistent acute rejection.10 Other therapies include the use of monoclonal or polyclonal antibodies, plas- mapheresis, and total lymphoid irradiation.10,13 Inhaled ciclosporin has also been used to treat refractory acute re- jection.1,10 Lung transplant recipients are at high risk of infection as a result of impaired pulmonary defence mechanisms, and post-transplant antibacterial prophylaxis is routine.2 1816 Immunosuppressants Patients at risk for CMV should be given ganciclovir.2,7,12 There is no consensus on standard antifungal prophylaxis after lung transplant, but some centres use oral azole ther- apy or inhaled amphotericin.2 Respiratory virus
